items.explanation: The title rabbi (Hebrew רַבִּי, 'my teacher') is not in the Torah. It becomes a formal title in the Mishnah period, after the destruction of the Second Temple. Moses is later called Moshe Rabbeinu, 'Moses our teacher', but that phrase comes from later tradition, not from the Torah text itself. In the Torah, Moses is called a prophet and a servant of God, not 'rabbi'.

later.note: Opens the chain of teaching from Moses to the later sages; it does not use 'rabbi' as a title for Moses.

items.explanation: The Torah never calls Moses 'Moshe Rabbeinu'. That honorary phrase, 'Moses our teacher', comes from later Jewish tradition. In the Torah Moses is called a prophet unlike any other, and a servant of the LORD, but not 'rabbi' or 'our teacher' as a title.

later.note: The honorary title Moshe Rabbeinu is used throughout later Jewish teaching; it is not a verse in the Torah.

items.explanation: The synagogue as a house of assembly and prayer is not described in the Torah. It develops later, especially after the Babylonian exile and in the Second Temple and rabbinic periods, as a place to gather, read Scripture and pray.

later.note: Rabbinic law about a synagogue (beit knesset) and its sanctity.

items.explanation: Hanukkah is not in the Torah, and it is not in the Tanakh either. It commemorates the rededication of the Temple in the days of the Maccabees, in the Second Temple period. The story is told in the Books of Maccabees and in later rabbinic sources, not in the Five Books of Moses.

later.note: The Talmud discusses why Hanukkah is observed and the miracle of the oil.

items.explanation: Purim is not in the Torah. The story of Esther, Mordecai and Haman, and the days of Purim, is in the Book of Esther, in the Writings (Ketuvim) of the Tanakh — after the Five Books of Moses.

later.note: Esther and Mordecai establish the days of Purim.

items.explanation: The Mishnah and the Talmud are not books of the Torah. Jewish tradition holds that an Oral Torah was given alongside the written Torah, and later sages organized that teaching in the Mishnah (about 200 CE) and discussed it in the Talmud. The written Torah itself does not name the Mishnah or the Talmud.

later.note: A later summary of the chain of teaching from Moses to the sages.

items.explanation: A bar or bat mitzvah ceremony is not in the Torah. Later Jewish law treats a boy as obligated in the commandments at thirteen and a girl at twelve, and communities developed ceremonies around that. The Torah itself does not describe this coming-of-age rite.

later.note: A later list of ages, including thirteen for the commandments.

items.explanation: The formal prayer quorum of ten adults, the minyan, is not stated in the Torah. It is a later rabbinic rule. The Torah does mention assemblies and a group of ten spies, but it does not set a rule of ten for public prayer.

later.note: Lists rites that require ten.

items.explanation: Kabbalah, including the Zohar, is later Jewish mystical teaching. It is not a book of the Torah and is not named in the Five Books of Moses. Some later writers read mystical meanings into Torah verses, but those systems come from medieval and earlier mystical tradition, not from the written Torah itself.

later.ref: later mystical tradition (not a Torah verse)
later.note: The Zohar and related works are medieval or later; they are not part of the Torah text.

items.explanation: The Torah commands a sacred day on the first of the seventh month, a day of sounding the horn (Yom Teruah). It does not call that day 'Rosh Hashanah' ('head of the year'). The familiar name and the idea of a new-year judgement day are developed in later tradition and appear in later books and in the Mishnah. The day itself — the first of the seventh month, with rest and the sounding of the horn — is in the Torah.

later.note: The Mishnah discusses the new years and the judgement of the world.

items.explanation: Simchat Torah, the celebration of finishing and restarting the annual Torah reading, is not in the Torah. It developed later, after the yearly reading cycle was fixed. The Torah does command the assembly at the end of the seventh month (Shemini Atzeret / the eighth-day gathering), which later calendars place beside Simchat Torah.

later.note: The celebration of completing the reading cycle is post-biblical.

items.explanation: The fast of Tisha B'Av is not commanded in the Torah. It later marks the destruction of the Temple, which the later historical books and Lamentations describe. The Torah itself does not name this fast.

later.note: Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem; it is in the Writings, not the Torah.
Lists calamities on the Ninth of Av.

items.explanation: Kol Nidrei is a later liturgical declaration at the start of Yom Kippur about vows. It is not a Torah passage. The Torah does discuss vows, and Yom Kippur itself is commanded in the Torah, but this particular text is later.

later.note: Kol Nidrei is a post-biblical prayer-house text.

items.explanation: The Torah commands binding 'these words' as a sign on the hand and as frontlets between the eyes. The later name tefillin, and the detailed form of the boxes and straps, come from the Oral Law and later codes. The underlying command is in the Torah; the later name and construction rules are not spelled out there.

later.note: Later law discusses tefillin by that name.

items.explanation: The Torah commands writing these words on the doorposts (mezuzot) of your house and on your gates. The later small parchment and case called a mezuzah, and the detailed rules for how it is written and placed, come from later law. The command to write the words on the doorposts is in the Torah.

later.ref: later law on the mezuzah scroll and case
later.note: The familiar case and parchment format are later specifications of the Torah's doorpost command.

items.explanation: The siddur (prayer book) and the formal Amidah of eighteen (later nineteen) blessings are not in the Torah. Daily and festival prayer took a fixed form in the rabbinic period. The Torah does speak of serving God, blessing, and moments of prayer by individuals, but it does not give this prayer-book.

later.note: Discusses the formal daily prayer.

items.explanation: The dreidel is a later Hanukkah custom. It is not in the Torah or the Tanakh.

later.note: A folk custom associated with Hanukkah, not a biblical command.

items.explanation: Wearing a kippah or yarmulke as everyday head covering is later custom, not a Torah command. The Torah describes special head coverings for priests in the sanctuary, which is a different matter.

later.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 31a (later discussion of covering the head)
later.note: Later discussion of head covering as reverence; not a Torah verse.

items.explanation: The Star of David (Magen David) as a Jewish symbol is not in the Torah. It becomes widely used much later. King David himself is a figure of the later historical books, not of the Torah's narrative after early genealogies.

later.note: The six-pointed star as a communal emblem is medieval and later.

items.explanation: David and Goliath are not in the Torah. The story is in the Book of Samuel, in the Prophets (Nevi'im) of the Tanakh. The Torah does mention a later descendant named David only in the sense that David lives long after Moses; he does not appear as a character in the Five Books.

later.note: The contest of David and Goliath.

items.explanation: The Book of Jonah is not part of the Torah. It is one of the Twelve Prophets, in the Nevi'im of the Tanakh.

later.note: Jonah in the fish; JPS 1917 numbering may place this as Jonah 1:17 in some English Bibles. The Hebrew book is in the Prophets, not the Torah.

items.explanation: The Psalms are not part of the Torah. They belong to the Writings (Ketuvim). Psalm 23, 'The LORD is my shepherd', is in that book, not in the Five Books of Moses.

later.note: A psalm in the Writings, not in the Torah.

items.explanation: The Book of Ruth is not part of the Torah. It is in the Writings (Ketuvim) of the Tanakh.

later.note: The opening of Ruth, in the Writings.

items.explanation: The Book of Esther is not part of the Torah. It is in the Writings (Ketuvim) of the Tanakh.

later.note: The opening of Esther.

items.explanation: The Book of Job is not part of the Torah. It is in the Writings (Ketuvim) of the Tanakh.

later.note: The opening of Job.

items.explanation: Daniel is not a figure of the Torah. The Book of Daniel, including the lions' den, is in the Writings (Ketuvim) of the Tanakh.

later.note: Daniel in the lions' den.

items.explanation: Elijah and Elisha are not in the Torah. Their stories are in the Books of Kings, in the Prophets.

later.note: The prophet Elijah is introduced in Kings, not in the Torah.

items.explanation: The Book of Isaiah is not part of the Torah. It is in the Prophets (Nevi'im).

later.note: The opening of Isaiah.

items.explanation: Hasidism is an early-modern Jewish movement, beginning in the 18th century. It is not in the Torah.

later.note: A much later movement in Jewish life.

items.explanation: The Torah does not teach a developed afterlife, a heaven-and-hell judgement, or 'olam haba' (the world to come). Those ideas are later. The Torah does mention Sheol, the nether-world, as the place of the dead (for example in Jacob's grief and in the Korah story). Resurrection of the dead is a later teaching, stated in the Mishnah, not in the Five Books.

later.note: Later rabbinic teaching on a share in the world to come and, in related discussion, resurrection.

terms: is there a messiah in the pentateuch
items.explanation: The later idea of the Messiah as a future saving king is not named in the Torah. In the Torah, mashiach (anointed) is used for a priest who is anointed, not for a coming king. Some later readers take Balaam's words about a star out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17) as messianic; the verse itself does not use the title Messiah. The hope for a future anointed king is developed in the Prophets and later tradition.

later.note: A later prophetic passage often read as messianic. It is not in the Five Books.

terms: snake in eden supposed to be satan
items.explanation: The figure called 'the Satan' (the accuser) is not in the Torah. That figure appears later, in books such as Job and Zechariah. The serpent in the Garden of Eden is never called Satan in the Torah text; later tradition sometimes identifies them. 'Lucifer' as a name is a later Latin reading of a passage in Isaiah, not a Torah verse.

later.note: The accuser (ha-satan) appears in Job, in the Writings, not in the Torah.
The accuser appears in Zechariah, in the Prophets.

terms: is jerusalem named in the torah
items.explanation: The name Jerusalem does not appear in the Torah. Places later linked with it do appear: Salem, whose king Melchizedek blesses Abram, and the land of Moriah, where Abraham binds Isaac. The city name Jerusalem is used in later books of the Tanakh, beginning with the Prophets.

later.note: The name Jerusalem is used in Joshua, which is in the Prophets, not the Torah.

items.explanation: Lilith is not in the Torah, and the Torah never describes a first wife of Adam besides the woman later named Eve. A word sometimes translated 'lilith' appears in Isaiah, in the Prophets, as a desert creature, not as Adam's wife. The story of Lilith as Adam's first wife is later midrash.

later.note: A later prophetic verse; it is not in the Torah and does not tell the midrashic Lilith story.

items.explanation: Reincarnation, or gilgul, is not taught in the Torah. It appears in later mystical teaching, not in the Five Books.

later.note: Gilgul is a later kabbalistic idea, not a Torah verse.

items.explanation: Original sin as a inherited fallen nature is a later Christian teaching, not a Torah term. The Torah does tell of the first man and woman eating from the tree and being sent from the garden, and of human wrongdoing, but it does not set out the later doctrine called original sin.

later.ref: later Christian theology (not a Torah source)
later.note: The doctrine is later and is not a Jewish Torah teaching.

items.explanation: The Trinity is a later Christian doctrine. It is not in the Torah. The Torah's central statement about God in the Shema is that the LORD is one.

later.ref: later Christian theology (not a Torah source)
later.note: The Trinity is not a teaching of the Torah.

items.explanation: Jesus is not mentioned in the Torah. The Five Books were written about events long before the first century. Later Christian readers have seen hints of him in various verses; those readings are later, not what the Torah text names.

later.ref: later Christian interpretation (not a Torah source)
later.note: The name and story of Jesus are not in the Torah.

terms: boil a kid in its mother's milk
items.explanation: The Torah three times says: you shall not seethe (boil) a kid in its mother's milk. That is a written Torah command. The later, broader rule of not eating any meat with any dairy, and of separate dishes, is how later Jewish law applies those verses. The full kitchen separation is later; the kid-in-milk prohibition is in the Torah.

later.ref: Mishnah Chullin 8:1-4 (later law on meat and milk)
later.note: Later rabbinic development of the Torah's kid-in-milk verses.

items.explanation: The Torah commands rest on the Sabbath and forbids work. It also says you shall kindle no fire in your dwellings on the Sabbath day, and it speaks of not cooking the manna on the Sabbath. Driving a car is not named, because it is a later technology; later law treats it as a question of work and fire. The written commands are rest, no work, and no kindling fire.

later.note: Later list of categories of work on Shabbat.

terms: giving of the torah on shavuot
shavuot is that when we got the torah
items.explanation: The Torah does command the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), a harvest festival of first fruits, counted seven weeks from the omer. The written Torah does not itself say that the Torah was given on that day. Linking Shavuot with the giving of the Torah at Sinai is later tradition. The festival is in the Torah; that historical association is later.

later.ref: later tradition linking Shavuot with the giving of the Torah
later.note: The identification of Shavuot as the anniversary of Sinai is post-biblical.

items.explanation: Genesis 18 says three men stood by Abraham and he hosted them; the chapter does not call those visitors angels. Genesis 19 then calls the visitors who went on to Sodom 'the two angels'. The visit itself is in the written Torah. Identifying Abraham's three guests as angels is a traditional reading of those chapters, not a word the Torah uses in Genesis 18.

later.ref: traditional identification of Abraham's three visitors as angels
later.note: Genesis 18 uses 'men'; later tradition commonly calls them angels.
